questions.question: How do you count words or character frequencies in Go?
questions.title: Count Words Go

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The word count, executed:

```go
words := strings.Fields("hello world go")
len(words)  // 3 — verified

// With a delimiter
parts := strings.Split("a,b,c", ",")
len(parts)  // 3
```

The character frequency counter:
```go
freq := make(map[rune]int)
for _, r := range "hello" { freq[r]++ }
// freq: h:1 e:1 l:2 o:1
```

The word-frequency counter (the composition):
```go
freq := make(map[string]int)
for _, w := range strings.Fields(text) {
    freq[strings.ToLower(w)]++  // case-normalized
}
```

The tools by job: Fields for word boundaries (whitespace runs — any space/tab/newline). Split for an exact delimiter. map[K]int for the count — the counter pattern from the hash-map topic. strings.ToLower for normalization, strings.TrimPunct for cleaning.

The counting idiom (the increment): freq[key]++ works on the zero value (an absent key reads as 0 — increment works without initialization). That single language feature is why the Go counter is one line.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T[text] --> F[strings.Fields] --> W[[]string words]
    W --> LEN[len — word count]
    W --> M[map[string]int — frequencies]
    S[string] --> R[for _, r := range s] --> RC[map[rune]int — char counts]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The Fields vs Split distinction (the DSA module's strings topic covers it deeper): Fields is the boundary-based splitter — any whitespace run is one separator, leading/trailing dropped. Split is the mark-based one — an exact string, with empty results between adjacent delimiters. Counting words = Fields; counting CSV fields = Split.

The rune iteration's correctness: for _, r := range s decodes UTF-8 as it iterates — the frequency counter is Unicode-correct (é counted once, not as two byte fragments). The byte form (for i := 0; i < len(s); i++) counts the ENCODING, not the characters — the strings topic's core distinction applied to counting.

The pattern's O: O(n) per pass (the split allocates the words; the counting builds the map). The space: the map's size is bounded by the distinct words/characters — for text processing, the map can approach n entries (all-unique words), which is honest: you can't count without remembering what you've seen.
